q: One radian, expressed in degrees, is approximately:
x: 1 rad = 180°/π ≈ 57.3° (about 57°17′45″). 0.0175 is the size of 1° in radians, the reverse conversion.

q: An arc of length 15 cm subtends an angle of 75° at the centre of a circle. What is the radius of the circle?
x: 75° = 75π/180 = 5π/12 rad, and r = l/θ = 15 ÷ (5π/12) = 36/π cm. Using θ = 75 without converting to radians gives 1/5 cm.

q: What is each interior angle of a regular hexagon in radians?
x: The interior angles of a hexagon add to (6 − 2) × 180° = 720°, so each is 120° = 2π/3. π/3 is the exterior angle.

q: A sector of a circle has arc length 6 cm and area 15 cm². What is its central angle?
x: Area = ½ r l gives 15 = ½ × r × 6, so r = 5 cm. Then θ = l/r = 6/5 rad. Inverting the ratio gives 5/6 rad.

q: A wheel of radius 35 cm rolls 11 m along level ground without slipping. Through what angle does it turn? (Take π = 22/7.)
x: The arc rolled out equals the distance: θ = 1100/35 = 220/7 rad. In degrees, 220/7 × 180/(22/7) = 1800°, which is 5 revolutions. Using the diameter instead of the radius gives 900°.

q: In two circles, arcs of the same length subtend angles of 60° and 75° at their centres. What is the ratio of the radius of the first circle to that of the second?
x: Equal arcs give r₁θ₁ = r₂θ₂, so r₁/r₂ = θ₂/θ₁ = 75/60 = 5/4. The radius is larger where the angle is smaller; 4 : 5 is the ratio of the angles, not the radii.

q: What is the value of cos 300°?
x: 300° = 360° − 60° lies in the fourth quadrant, where cosine is positive, so cos 300° = cos 60° = 1/2. Taking the fourth-quadrant sign as negative gives −1/2.

q: What is the value of sec 30° · cosec 60° + cot 45°?
x: sec 30° = 2/√3 and cosec 60° = 2/√3, so their product is 4/3; adding cot 45° = 1 gives 7/3. Forgetting the cot 45° term leaves 4/3.

q: The terminal side of an angle θ (0 ≤ θ < 2π) lies along the line y = −√3x in the second quadrant. What is θ?
x: The point (−1, √3) lies on the line in the second quadrant, so tan θ = −√3 with θ in quadrant II, giving θ = π − π/3 = 2π/3. 5π/3 is the same line in the fourth quadrant.

q: What is the value of sin 420° cos 390° + cos(−300°) sin(−330°)?
The angles are in radians. Which of these has the greatest value?
x: 1 rad ≈ 57°, 2 rad ≈ 115°, 3 rad ≈ 172° and 4 rad ≈ 229°. sin 2 = sin(180° − 115°) = sin 65° is larger than sin 57°; sin 3 = sin 8° is small and sin 4 is negative. Reading the angles as degrees would wrongly pick sin 4.

q: For angles where it is defined, (sec²θ − 1) cos²θ simplifies to:
x: sec²θ − 1 = tan²θ, and tan²θ · cos²θ = (sin²θ/cos²θ) · cos²θ = sin²θ. Stopping at sec²θ − 1 = tan²θ gives the tan²θ slip.

q: For every θ, sin⁶θ + cos⁶θ + 3 sin²θ cos²θ equals:
x: With a = sin²θ and b = cos²θ, a³ + b³ = (a + b)³ − 3ab(a + b) = 1 − 3ab. Adding 3ab gives 1. Check θ = 0: 0 + 1 + 0 = 1.

q: For angles where it is defined, (1 + tan²θ)/(1 + cot²θ) simplifies to:
x: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ, so the quotient is sec²θ/cosec²θ = sin²θ/cos²θ = tan²θ. Check θ = 45°: 2/2 = 1 = tan²45°, and at θ = 60°: 4/(4/3) = 3 = tan²60°.

q: If 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ = 5, what is the value of tan θ?
x: Put 4 cos θ = 5 − 3 sin θ and square: 16(1 − sin²θ) = 25 − 30 sin θ + 9 sin²θ, so 25 sin²θ − 30 sin θ + 9 = 0, i.e. (5 sin θ − 3)² = 0. Then sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5 and tan θ = 3/4. 4/3 swaps sine and cosine.

q: If cos θ − sin θ = √2 sin θ, then cos θ + sin θ equals:
x: From the condition, cos θ = (√2 + 1) sin θ, so sin θ = (√2 − 1) cos θ after rationalising. Then cos θ + sin θ = cos θ + (√2 − 1) cos θ = √2 cos θ.
